extracted.intended_audience: educated English readers interested in literature, manners, travel, and conduct (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance for composing short moral/literary essays, translations, and conduct pieces in the Spectator tradition; also prescriptive advice for social behaviour (travel, marriage ceremonies, seasonal conduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel as means to improve taste for the ancients
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving our Taste of the best Authors of Antiquity, by seeing the Places where they lived, and of which they wrote; to compare the natural Face of the Country with the Descriptions they have given us, and observe how well the Picture agrees with the Original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing the actual places makes reading authors a "most charming Exercise"; compare landscape to literary description; examine spots celebrated as scenes of famous actions (Cato, Cicero, Brutus) to warm a generous mind and inspire imitation of virtues; but this benefit presumes the traveller can enter into the sense and spirit of the ancients (knowing their language/first principles). Example/anti-pattern: meaningless sightseeing by those ignorant of classical language yields only vanity ("to build a gawdy Structure without any Foundation").

rubrics_metrics.name: Know native customs and first principles before adopting cosmopolitan manners
rubrics_metrics.description: How can any of these Advantages be attained by one who is a mere Stranger to the Customs and Policies of his native Country, and has not yet fixed in his Mind the first Principles of Manners and Behaviour? To endeavour it, is to build a gawdy Structure without any Foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to assume polite/cosmopolitan behaviour by imitation alone; first learn your own country's manners and basic principles of behaviour. Anti-pattern: attempting a "rich Embroidery upon a Cobweb"—superficial polish without foundational knowledge is ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautions about sending young/inexperienced people abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Though to be Sea-sick, or jumbled in an outlandish Stage-Coach, may perhaps be healthful for the Constitution of the Body, yet it is apt to cause such a Dizziness in young empty Heads, as too often lasts their Life-time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn parents/guardians against showing young, inexperienced persons as a ridiculous spectacle abroad; travel can leave lasting negative effects on impressionable minds. Practical admonition: avoid exposing young naive travellers to foreign fashions/behaviour until grounded in native customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal conduct rules for women (May Caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and Directions for their better avoiding those Calentures which are so very frequent in this Season: do not venture abroad in the Fields, but in the Company of a Parent, a Guardian, or some other sober discreet Person; have a spare and simple Diet, with the moderate Use of Phlebotomy; be careful how they meddle with Romances, Chocolate, Novels, and the like Inflamers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prescriptions to resist May inclinations: avoid solitary rural amusements (May-poles, green gown ceremonies), prefer Tragedy to Comedy at the playhouse, puppet-shows are safer than the Opera while the Sun is in Gemini; remember the month is short (31 days) so endure it. Anti-patterns: giving up to nature (prostitutes make no distinction between months). The guidance blends medical/astrological, moral, and cultural recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony and decorum at marriage — avoid warlike music
rubrics_metrics.description: These warlike Sounds (methinks) are very improper in a Marriage-Consort, and give great Offence; they seem to insinuate, that the Joys of this State are short, and that Jars and Discord soon ensue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request to silence drums at dawn after a wedding so that soft airs may usher in a bridal morning; social-ceremony music should be appropriate to the occasion and not suggest ominous meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment in love-writing must arise from occasion; avoid ostentatious wit
rubrics_metrics.description: When this Passion is represented by Writers, ... the most absurd of all things is to be witty; every Sentiment must grow out of the Occasion, and be suitable to the Circumstances of the Character. Where this Rule is transgressed, the humble Servant, in all the fine things he says, is but shewing his Mistress how well he can dress, instead of saying how well he loves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portraying love (songs, letters, lyric), prioritize natural tender sentiment over clever turns; avoid lace-and-drapery (ornamental language) that shows skill rather than passion. Keep voice and tone appropriate to character and situation; example: a servant's fine phrases are an anti-pattern if they do not spring from genuine occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity coupled with formal adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: I have faithfully kept to the Sentiments, without adding or diminishing; ... The Numbers in the Original are as loose and unequal ... I have ventured to bind it in stricter Measures, as being more proper for our Tongue, tho perhaps wilder Graces may better suit the Genius of the Laponian Language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators should preserve the original's sentiments (no adding/diminishing), but adapt form (measure/meter) to suit the target language's proprieties; recognize trade-offs: preserving spirit vs keeping original formal idiosyncrasies. Example: keep sentiment faithful; modify versification when necessary for the English ear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for heroic/epic poetry (composition and critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Heroick Poem, according to the Opinion of the best Criticks, ought to end happily, and leave the Mind of the Reader, after having conducted it through many Doubts and Fears, Sorrows and Disquietudes, in a State of Tranquility and Satisfaction. Milton's mixture of Vision and Narrative is a defect where the Narration flags; the exhibiting part in vision is preferable to narrative where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for judging/composing epic: (1) prefer exhibited/visual scenes to long narration where poetical ornamentation is possible; (2) keep the poetic mode consistent—avoid switching to merely narrative prose that weakens effect; (3) end the epic happily to restore reader's tranquility; (4) use strong, vivid poetical images for episodes (Babel, Plagues, Storms) and avoid allowing theological/discursive attention to drown poetic quality. Anti-pattern: excessive doctrinal or expository digression that neglects poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of moral resolution in epic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton leaves the Adversary of Mankind ... under the lowest State of Mortification and Disappointment. On the contrary, our two first Parents are comforted by Dreams and Visions, cheared with Promises of Salvation ... The last Speeches of Adam and the Arch-Angel are full of Moral and Instructive Sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In heroic narrative, artists should give moral closure: antagonists humbled and protagonists elevated morally; conclude with instructive, consolatory speeches that reinforce the poem's moral design and leave readers uplifted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnanimity and composure as standards of heroic character in life-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Her Behaviour was so magnanimous throughout this whole Affair ... She possessed her Mind with so wonderful a Patience ... Such Greatness was not to be acquired in her last Article, nor is it to be doubted but it was a constant Practice of all that is praise-worthy, which made her capable of beholding Death...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing biographical sketches or moral exempla, foreground virtues of magnanimity, composure under pain, generosity (forgiving or rewarding those who erred), and habitual practice of praise-worthy conduct rather than sudden conversion. Use detailed anecdote and direct speech to illustrate moral character.
